judgements.rationale: Both decks are free of clipping, placeholders or overlap, so the split is decided at levels 3–5. A is stronger at communicative effectiveness and craft. On A, slide 3 the bar chart carries a right-hand annotation column that names each division's return and share of capital (19% highest return, 22% of capital; 6% lowest), so the chart makes its own argument; A slide 5 and 6 pair full tables with a highlighted callout box (11.8% blended current vs 14.3% returns-led), and slide 6 shows a signed delta column (+19.2 / -19.2 / +19.6) that is the actual answer to 'what would a returns-led allocation look like'. A slide 9 puts the +2.5 pts and 'EUR 0 additional capital required' callouts beside the glide-path line, and slide 8's three-year table includes a footnote on the maths. A slide 7 states the five constraints as bolded label + explanation with a summarising implication line at the foot, and slide 10 ends with a bolded closing line plus a numbered ask. B answers the same brief more thinly: its slide 2 executive summary is three sparse bullets floating in a mostly empty page, slide 3's grouped bar chart shows revenue share vs capital allocated but the key series — return on incremental capital — is relegated to a caption reading 'Not shown: return on incremental capital', which is a self-declared miss on the deck's central variable; slide 5 is a dense six-column table with no takeaway; slide 8's stacked columns are unlabelled beyond tiny segment values and it is hard to read the shift from FY26 to FY29; slide 10 closes with three plain bullets. B's chart axes are also mostly unlabelled and units are inconsistent (bps on 9, € elsewhere). Coherence: A repeats a kicker/title/rule system and a consistent callout-card motif; B is also consistent (green rule, running footer, page numbers) and its typographic restraint is arguably cleaner, and B's monospaced footer is a genuine identity touch — but B's whitespace on slides 1, 2 and 10 reads as underfilled rather than composed. Both are recognisably corporate-consultant templates; neither is distinctive, but A does more with the space and would need less rework before going to a board.

Integrity: both render without clipping, but B page 3 is broken as data — a grouped bar chart of 'Revenue share' vs 'Capital allocated' whose bars are 32/32, 28/29, 24/24, 15/15, i.e. two nearly identical series, and the page title claims '€120m is allocated roughly in line with revenue' while the footnote admits the actual subject (return on incremental capital, 6%-19%) is 'Not shown'. The page spends its whole area proving a non-point and defers the argument. A page 4 handles the same idea correctly: capital share vs incremental return side by side, with two callouts naming Division C (26% of capital → 6% return) and D (15% → 14%). Legibility: B's body text is uniformly tiny — the bullets on pages 2 and 10 are set at what looks like 8-9pt on a board slide, and the table type on pages 5 and 6 is smaller still; A uses a readable bold-lead-in bullet structure on pages 2 and 7 and larger table type. Coherence: both are consistent, but B's page 9 mixes a line chart with two oversized statistic blocks ('+190 bps', '~ €2.3m') at wildly different type scales against a chart whose axis labels are near-invisible; A's page 9 pairs the same line with two matched bordered stat cards ('+2.5 pts', 'EUR 0'). Communicative effectiveness is where the gap becomes decisive: A's tables carry units in the headers ('Capital allocated (EURm)', 'Returns-led allocation (EURm)', 'Δ vs current (EURm)'), totals rows that reconcile to 120.0, a signed delta column, and a source/assumption note under page 5 and page 8; B's tables on pages 5 and 6 mix €m and % without a units row, and page 6's 'Change' column (+€16m, +€6m, -€6m, -€29m) sits under a title that says the allocation would 'zero out Division C' while the table still shows Division C at €0 — internally consistent only if you read the fine print. B page 8's stacked columns have no axis, no units and a legend of four undifferentiated divisions, so the glide path is unreadable; A page 8 states the same glide path as a table with Current/Year 1/Year 2/Year 3 columns and a total that holds at 120.0. A's page 7 gives five named constraints with reasoning and a synthesised implication line; B's page 7 gives four two-line boxes. A page 10 ends with four numbered, specific approvals plus a closing line; B page 10 gives three bullets in 8pt. Craft: A page 1 opens with three framed metric chips (EUR 120m / 4 / 6%-19%) that set up the whole argument; B page 1 is a title and subtitle on white. Both are recognisably consultant-deck generic, but A is the one that is actually finished. B's failure is at level 4 and partly at level 2, so no amount of its cleaner chart styling rescues it.

Both decks are structurally sound and free of clipping or placeholder text, so the decision turns on legibility and communicative effectiveness, where A holds a narrow lead. B's slide 2 — the load-bearing 'why now' evidence — squeezes the EBITDA line chart into the left half with roughly ten y-axis tick labels crammed together and both series flattened against the top of the plot, so the six-point divergence the title claims is not visible in the mark; A's slide 3 renders the same story as a clearly diverging red line against a flat peer line with a large '-6 pts' callout and a legible note on the peer baseline. B's slide 5 governance boxes (five owner cards with name, workstream and EUR value) and the italic grey footnote on slide 9 sit at type sizes that will not read at the back of a room of twenty. B's slide 4 bar chart also ships without value labels and with category names set far left of the bars, duplicating the table beside it, and its accountability content spills across slides 8 and 9 with only two owner rows each and large empty bands, reading as overflow rather than a decision; the closing slide 12 date cards are mostly empty dark boxes with text pinned to the top. Where B is stronger is coherence and distinctiveness: its monochrome palette, consistent eyebrow labels and dark open/close bookends look authored, and it adds a risks-and-dependencies slide A omits. A pays for its readability with generic choices — an arbitrary multicolour bar chart on slide 5 (blue/orange/green/yellow with no encoding meaning), a SmartArt-style org chart on slide 7, and blue/orange/green phase cards on slide 9 that break its otherwise blue palette. Since a legibility failure outranks a craft advantage, A edges it, but only slightly, and A is by far the more generic of the two — its agenda circles, three-card row and stoplight phase cards would look identical for any other programme, whereas B's typographic restraint is at least specific to this document.

Integrity: both decks render fully — no clipping or placeholder text — but B's accountability pair is close to a failure of intent: slide 8 carries only two workstream rows (Procurement, Manufacturing Footprint) stranded in a half-empty table with a large blank band, and slide 9 wedges the grey italic note 'All five owners report progress...' between two more rows, so a single table has been split badly across two pages with mismatched density. A puts all five owners, targets and dates on one table (slide 10) with even row rhythm. Legibility, the level that decides this: B runs very small type in exactly the places that carry the argument — the EBITDA-margin chart on slide 2 has axis and legend labels at near-footnote size and the takeaway 'The gap to peers has widened from 0.6 points to 5.1 points' is small grey italic; the slide 4 workstream bar chart has hairline category labels; the slide 6 cadence table and slide 10 risk table are set at body-note scale. For twenty people in a kickoff room, A's larger table text, labelled axes and legends (slide 3 line chart with the red '-6 pts' callout, slide 5 bar chart with '€40M' anchor) hold up better. Coherence and craft run the other way: B is the more disciplined document — one monochrome system, consistent eyebrow labels ('WHY NOW', 'THE TARGET', 'GOVERNANCE'), the black cover answered by the black closing slide 12, and conclusion titles ('We have lost six margin points in two years — peers have not', 'Four cadences keep EUR 40m of savings on track'). A is competent but visibly stock: rainbow bar colours on slide 5 that encode nothing, phase cards on slide 9 recoloured blue/orange/green for decoration, a cover whose blue block stops short of the right edge leaving dead white, and an agenda slide that spends a page on nothing. Communicatively they are close — both have units and takeaways, A adds a Total row on slide 6 that B lacks. A wins narrowly because its level-2 and layout-integrity advantages outrank B's clear superiority in coherence and distinctiveness. On genericness: A would look identical for any other cost programme; B is unmistakably made for this brief.

Both decks are clean at the integrity level — nothing is clipped or left as placeholder in either — so the decision is made at levels 3–5. A's charts break coherence and communication: on page 4 the bar chart's y-axis is unlabeled numeric ticks (0–5) with the axis title 'Weeks' rotated and cramped, the '2' and '5' data labels float above bars with no unit, and on page 8 the y-axis reads '% of lost-deal reasons' but the bars are labeled 40 and 11 while the tick labels run 0%–45% in a duplicated scale; the legend 'Believed by sales / Actual (survey)' sits under a chart whose title ('Pricing is not the objection sales believes it is') is a claim the chart supports but never states as a takeaway on the chart itself. A also leans on oversized standalone stat blocks (+125% on p4, #1 on p6, '40% vs 11%' on p8) parked beside a wall of body text, which reads as a template pattern rather than a designed argument. A's page 3 uses three numbered cards (01/02/03) whose text overflows into ragged multi-line runs of different lengths, leaving uneven grey boxes.

B is tighter on the same material. Page 3 replaces the three unequal cards with a clean numbered list, so the three themes read at a glance. Page 4 pairs the promised-vs-actual bar chart with a verbatim customer quote ('I was still configuring integrations when my trial urgency wore off') and an attribution line, giving the chart a human takeaway; page 6 does the same with a ranked list of retention reasons plus a quote. Page 8's chart carries an explicit source line ('Source: win-loss coding on closed-lost deals'), which A's equivalent chart lacks entirely. B's implication slides (5, 7, 9) use short spaced bullets rather than A's dense five-line paragraphs, and B's titles are more conclusive ('Onboarding takes 4.5 weeks. We promise two.', 'Stop discounting reflexively — diagnose the other 89%') than A's ('Onboarding takes more than double what we promise'). B's summary table on page 10 adds a Priority column with High/High/Medium, which A's table omits.

Against that, B has real flaws: the title slide (p1) has a large empty upper third that reads as unresolved, and B's charts still label bars with bare numbers (40, 11) whose unit lives only on the axis. Both decks are typographically generic — Helvetica-ish sans, black-on-white, one accent-free palette — and neither would look out of place for a different brief; B is marginally less so because the quotes and ranked lists are shaped by this content. B wins clearly on communicative effectiveness (sourcing, takeaways, scannable implications) with no offsetting failure at a lower level.

Both decks are clean at Level 1-2 with one integrity blemish each: in A the slide 4 chart legend ('Promised/Actual' swatches under a 'Weeks to onboard' axis) and the slide 8 dual-series legend are cramped at very small type, and A's slide 1 leaves a lot of dead space between the subtitle and the thin footer line; in B the slide 4 chart y-axis runs -0.5 to 5 with a needless negative region below the bars, and B's slide 5 and 9 bullet blocks sit as a small text column against a large empty right half. Neither clips or overlaps. They diverge at Level 4. A's titles conclude: 'Onboarding takes more than double what we promise', 'Roadmap: close the onboarding gap before it costs the account', 'Redirect the story sales tells — and the effort behind it'. B's titles are closer to labels ('Three patterns cut across both datasets', 'Stop discounting reflexively — diagnose the other 89%' is the exception). A pairs every chart with a stated number and a written takeaway: slide 4 shows '+125%' with the sentence explaining onboarding delay as the most-cited churn reason; slide 8 shows '40% vs 11%' with the interpretation that pricing accounts for a quarter of what sales believes; slide 6 shows '#1 most-cited reason' with the survey caveat. B's slide 4 chart has a callout quote but no derived number, and B's slide 8 caption is smaller and less pointed. A's slide 3 uses three numbered evidence cards, each with the finding and its qualifier ('The single largest driver of early churn'), against B's slide 3 which is a bare three-line numbered list on a mostly empty page. A's slide 10 table has a black header row and a Finding/Evidence/Roadmap priority structure; B's slide 10 table adds a Priority column but its cells are dense, small and grey. A also carries running slide numbers ('4 / 11') and a consistent footer, which B lacks. At Level 5, A's asymmetric chart-plus-big-number compositions on 4, 6 and 8 look composed for this material; B's slides 5, 7 and 9 are the same left-aligned bullet list three times with no visual differentiation, which is where B reads more like a filled-in template. A is not distinctive either — the eyebrow/title/body skeleton is stock — but it varies its page types to the content. A wins clearly on communicative effectiveness.

Neither deck has an integrity failure I can see — no clipping, no placeholder text — so the decision is made at levels 3–5. On coherence, A repeats a real system: an eyebrow kicker on every slide (EXECUTIVE SUMMARY, THE COST OF STANDING STILL, GOVERNANCE & FUNDING GATES), a rule under the title, a consistent stat-box row (slides 2, 3, 15), and a footer with running title and page number. B repeats only a title and a footer; everything below the title is improvised per slide. B's biggest weakness is density discipline: slide 7 ('Age, Cost and People Are Converging on One Window') is three short bullets and one sentence with the bottom two-thirds of the slide empty, and slides 11 and 13 have the same problem — an investment committee page carrying almost no content. Slide 15's two stat boxes float in a large empty band. A holds a stable text block across all 15 pages. On communicative effectiveness A is also ahead: its titles carry the conclusion ('Doing nothing still costs EUR 25m over six years — and that is the conservative number', 'Cumulative value turns positive in year six, then compounds'), and its charts carry footnote/source lines (slide 9 'Illustrative annual phasing of the EUR 23m investment…', slide 10 'Net of the EUR 23m investment…'). A also answers parts of the brief B under-serves: slide 7's alternatives matrix with a Recommendation row, slide 12's gate table with timing/release/approval criteria, and two separate risk slides (13 risks with likelihood/impact, 14 with owner and mitigation). B compresses alternatives into one table (slide 6) and risks into one (slide 12). One chart choice in B is actively wrong: slide 5 plots five discrete engineers as a continuous line, implying fractional headcount; A uses a bar chart for the same data. B is not bad — it is clean, legible and consistently footed — but it reads as a default template with the blanks filled in, whereas A's dark cover, kicker system and stat-box language read as composed for this brief. A also lands closer to the edge on type size (the right-hand bullets on slide 5 and the risk tables on 13–14 are small), which is why this is clear rather than decisive. I would send A with light edits; I would send B only after rebuilding slides 7, 11 and 13.

Both decks are structurally complete at 15 slides and neither shows clipping, empty frames or placeholder text, so integrity and legibility are broadly satisfied on both — but A holds a higher bar from level 2 upward. Legibility: B sets its body copy very small relative to the frame (slides 2, 3, 11, 13 are thin bullet lists floating in large white space) and B's slide 6 alternatives table crams five columns of fine print with a red 'Recommended' cell as the only emphasis; A gives its equivalent table (slide 7) larger cells and reserves its emphasis for a single bolded 'Recommended' row, and A's slide 8 replaces the dense table with six checkmarked criteria lines that are readable at committee distance. Coherence: A repeats a disciplined kicker system on every slide ('EXECUTIVE SUMMARY', 'THE RETIREMENT CLOCK', 'THE COST OF STANDING STILL') above a sentence-case headline plus a rule, and repeats the footer/pagination identically; B's headline block sits alone with no eyebrow, and B's slide sizes drift — the KPI strip on slide 2 is a light grey chip row while the identical device on slide 15 is only two chips, unanchored and centred, leaving a large dead band beneath. B's slide 10 phase bars are three flat rectangles of arbitrary greys with the labels crushed inside them; A's slide 11 renders the same phasing as three bounded phase cards with per-phase deliverables and a labelled gate strip above, which is the more informative and more composed treatment. Communicative effectiveness is where the gap widens: A's titles state the conclusion ('Waiting doesn't reduce the risk. It concentrates it.', 'Cumulative value turns positive in year six, then compounds', 'Capital releases in three tranches, each earned, not assumed'), and A's charts carry both a takeaway note and a stated assumption footnote (slide 5 'Assumes a flat EUR 4.2m a year', slide 10 'Net of the EUR 23m investment'); B's titles are more descriptive ('Costs More Upfront, Less Within Five Years', 'Thirty Months, Three Phases, Each With a Gate') and its charts on slides 4, 8 and 9 have unlabelled or unitless axes — slide 8's bar chart has a bare numeric axis with no currency unit, and slide 5's retirement chart plots 'Engineers' against Now/Year 1-4 without saying that the line is a headcount decline from five. A also adds a genuine risk pairing (slide 13 risk/likelihood/impact/why it matters, slide 14 owner and mitigation for each of the same five risks), where B compresses risk and mitigation into one three-column table on slide 12 with wrapped mitigation prose that runs to four lines per cell. Craft: A's black title slide with the kicker, rule and confidential line reads as an authored cover; B's opening slide is left-aligned grey type on white that reads as an unstyled default. Neither is bespoke — both are near-monochrome grey/black business decks, and A's black cover plus red 'Recommended' accent is the only real colour decision in either — so both remain fairly generic, but A is the one I would send with my name on it. Clear, not decisive: B is clean and error-free, it simply concludes less and composes less.

Both clear level 1: no clipping, no placeholders, no empty frames in either. Level 2 separates them slightly. A is legible throughout — body text on slides 7/8/9 and the tables on 6, 12, 14 sit at comfortable board-projection sizes. B pushes far more copy into small type: the four risk lines on slide 13 and the three numbered asks on 14 are set at a size that reads as a document, not a projected deck, and the 6-column table on slide 12 (Share / 6M / Confidence / Investment / Time to impact) is the smallest type in either deck. B's black chapter dividers (3, 7, 11) and closing 'Thank you' also spend 4 of 15 slides on near-content-free pages, which is a communicative cost, not a legibility failure. Level 3: B is arguably the more disciplined system — the eyebrow rule, the persistent '01/15 — GROWTH PLAN · BOARD READOUT' footer, and the repeated 41/34/25 share bar on slides 8, 9, 10 are genuinely consistent, and A's slide 10 bubble matrix (axis labels 'Quick wins', 'Foundational...') is the one element in A that looks hand-placed and does not reuse the deck's colour logic. Level 4 is where A wins the document. A's titles conclude: 'Expansion is the largest, safest lever: EUR 38m from a 22% attach rate', 'Expansion is the best risk-adjusted bet', 'Two of the three levers need the board's approval to move'. B's titles mostly label: 'Two adjacent segments: 34% of the plan', 'Pricing: 25% of the plan'. A's slide 2 executive summary is a genuine standalone read — a 5-column table with share, contribution, confidence and investment plus an explicit 'THE ASK' line — where B's slide 2 summary is three bullets and a one-line ask. A also carries the brief's numbers with units in more places (slide 5 bridge with a 'Figures in millions' note, slide 11 stacked phasing with the cumulative EUR 250m/281m/310m callout, slide 14 checkpoint table with the FY27/28/29 proof points), and A's colour coding of the three levers (navy/teal/orange/indigo) does real work: the same lever keeps the same colour on 5, 6, 10, 12, 13. B's greyscale bridge on slide 6 is handsome but its 'Darker accent = higher confidence' encoding is invented and hard to decode, and B has no risk-mitigation pairing — slide 13 lists four risks with no owner or countermeasure, where A's slide 12 table pairs each lever's risk with a mitigation. Level 5: B is the more distinctive object — the oversized numerals, the black chapters, the rule-and-eyebrow system look designed. A is closer to a competent consulting template, and its slide 13 approval cards are plain outlined boxes. So B wins on craft and A wins on communication, but the rubric ranks legibility and effectiveness first, and A's small type never gets as small as B's slides 12–14. Net: A is the one to send, but only slightly — B is one editing pass on type size and title verbs from being the better deck.

Both decks are clean and free of clipping, so the decision turns on levels 3–5. B is coherent but bare: its charts and tables are the weak point. The page-6 waterfall in B has grey-on-grey bars with a caption that has to explain 'Darker accent = higher confidence' — a legend doing work the encoding should do — and its axis labels ('TODAY, EXPANSION - 41%, ADJACENT - 34%, PRICING - 25%, PLAN (FY29)') repeat percentages already stated three slides earlier. B's page 12 table is the only place confidence and investment are compared, and it is set in tiny type with an odd hanging 'Time to impact' column header. B also spends three full slides (3, 7, 11) on black chapter dividers with giant '01/02/03' numerals — a fifth of a 15-slide board deck on navigation, which is density misjudged for the purpose. A carries more argument per page: the page-2 executive summary is a genuine standalone table (lever, share, 6M, confidence, investment) closing with a bolded 'THE ASK', which is exactly what the brief asked for. A's bridge on page 5 uses distinct colours per lever with a labelled axis strip beneath ('Today €218m / Expansion +€38m (41%) / Adjacent segments +€31m (34%) / Pricing +€23m (25%) / Plan €310m'), so the chart carries its own reading. A also adds analysis B does not attempt: the page-10 risk/investment bubble quadrant, the page-11 stacked phasing chart with a cumulative-revenue footnote, and a page-14 checkpoint table tying FY27/FY28/FY29 to proof points. A's titles are conclusions ('Expansion is the best risk-adjusted bet', 'Expansion leads early; segments scale through year three'), where B's are labels ('How €92M closes: three sources, three levers', 'What would break the plan'). A's colour discipline — navy base with a per-lever green/orange/blue that recurs on pages 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 — is the kind of repeated element that reads as designed rather than filled in; B's monochrome is defensible but generic, and its page-13 risk bullets use four differently shaded squares with no key. Against A: page 10's bubble chart is the loosest element in either deck ('Quick wins' / 'Costly, uncertain' corner labels are small and the axis captions are faint), and page 6's 'Every dollar of new revenue splits three ways' is a table doing a chart's job. Neither is fatal. A wins clearly on levels 4 and 5 with parity below.

Both decks are structurally complete and free of gross integrity failures, so the decision turns on levels 2–5. A's advantage is legibility: its type is larger and its stat blocks (slide 3, slide 7's giant '11', slide 8's '4') read instantly. B pushes type smaller — the footers and the slide 6 axis-panel body are very small, and the slide 8/9/10/11 tables are dense — but the headline and column type still hold at presentation size, and B's tables are cleanly ruled with unit-bearing column heads ('€m / yr', 'Revenue €m', 'Current €m/yr', 'Proposed €m/yr'). A's slide 10 reallocation table, by contrast, has ragged unlabelled columns ('Today (est., €M/yr)', 'Tomorrow (est., €M/yr)') and a 'Total' row of 18.0 → 18.0 that is stated but never reconciled, plus the caption admits the figures are 'illustrative — provided by project count'. Level 4 is where B pulls ahead decisively. B names actual projects (Atlas, Meridian, Solstice, Vantage, Beacon, Tundra on slide 8; Orbit, Compass, Ferrum, Solace on slide 9; Vireo, Kestrel, Sable, Marlin on slide 10) with per-project euro figures — the deck reads as a real portfolio review. A never names a single project across twelve slides; slides 7, 8 and 9 are a big number plus four generic bullets ('Each has consumed a full year of budget without reaching the market'), which is assertion, not evidence. B's titles also conclude harder: 'Half the portfolio's cash is trapped in projects that will not pay it back', 'The board approved 50/30/20. The portfolio runs 78/15/7', 'Eleven projects, €9.6m a year, three years of runway with nothing to show'. A's are closer to labels ('Three clusters, three decisions', 'The portfolio mapped'). B's slide 4 chart carries a source line ('Source: FY2026 portfolio ledger — annual spend by maturity segment'); A's slide 4 chart carries only an ambition footnote and no source. B's slide 12 is a dated 30-day execution plan with owners implied; A's slide 12 is three approval asks. On coherence both are consistent, though B's slide 6 leaves a large empty band under the two axis panels and above the STOP/FUND/HOLD strip, and its slide 7 bubble map is faint compared to A's cleaner quadrant on slide 6 — A's map is the better single artefact. On distinctiveness, A's blue/red/green title-and-accent system is competent but reads as a standard consulting template with the blanks filled; B's near-black cover, restrained rules and vermilion/olive accents feel more authored, and the named projects mean the deck could not be dropped onto another brief unchanged. B is what I would send, after tightening the footer size and the slide 6 whitespace.

Integrity: both render cleanly with no clipping, empty frames or placeholder text; A's slide 10 table and B's slides 8-10 tables all fit. No level-1 failure either way. Legibility: A is safer at small sizes (large blue KPI numerals on 1 and 3, generous 12-16pt body), while B runs genuinely small type in several places — the two-column bullet blocks on 8/9/10, the axis labels and legend on 4/5, and the footer rules on 2 — and B's slide 6 quadrant legend ('Stop = 11 · €9.6m/yr  Fund = 4 · €5.4m/yr  Hold = 8 · €3.0m/yr') is near-unreadable at deck scale. That is B's one real cost. Visual coherence: B is markedly more disciplined — a consistent left-aligned eyebrow + sentence-case headline on every slide, a single rule-and-footer system, one restrained palette (black/red/green/ochre) used semantically (red = stop on 8, green = fund on 9, ochre = hold on 10, and the same three colours reused as the bubbles on the map on 7). A drifts: the blue KPI band on 3 uses five different accent colours for the same five numbers with no semantic logic, slide 5's two grey 'axis' cards and slide 11's three numbered cards are a different card idiom from the rest, and the recurring full-width blue callout bars (2, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11) are a template device applied by rote rather than by argument. Communicative effectiveness: both title in conclusions, but B's are sharper and carry the number and the verdict together — 'Half the portfolio's cash is trapped in projects that will not pay it back', 'The board approved 50/30/20. The portfolio runs 78/15/7', 'Eleven projects, €9.6m a year, three years of runway with nothing to show'. B also does the analytic work A skips: slide 6 states the methodology (the two axes and the STOP/FUND/HOLD decision rule) before slide 7 plots it, slide 11 reconciles the €18m before-and-after with a change column and a footnote on rounding, and the tables on 8/9/10 name every project with its €m/yr so the recommendation is auditable. A asserts the same conclusions but shows only aggregate counts — its slide 10 table lists budgets and 'moves' but never names a project, so the 11 to stop are never identifiable. A's slide 5 axis cards restate the axes in prose without a plot; B's slide 4 bar chart carries a source line ('Source: FY2026 portfolio ledger'), which A's chart on 4 lacks. Craft and distinctiveness: B reads as made for this brief — the black cover, the map on 7 with weighted bubbles positioned on real axes, the per-decision tables. A reads as a competent corporate template with the blanks filled: numbered blue chips on 2, the KPI strip on 3, the three-card 'rule' row on 11, the blue closing 'Approve the three moves' slide. Verdict: A wins on legibility only in the small-type sense, and B's slide 6 legend is the one place I would fix before sending, but B wins coherence, evidence and distinctiveness by a wide enough margin that it is the deck I would put my name on.

Both decks clear integrity — nothing clipped, no placeholders, ten slides each with sources and takeaway-style titles — so the decision falls to levels 2–4. On legibility, A runs consistently smaller: the axis ticks, category labels and rotated 'EUR mln' axis title on slides 4–6 are near-vanishing, the donut legend on slide 7 is barely readable, and the paragraph text inside the three coloured criteria blocks on slide 7 and the three outcome boxes on slide 10 is set at caption size for projection. B's equivalent elements (the criteria/weights table on slide 3, the comparison table on slide 4, the three cards on slides 7 and 10) are set larger and with more air. On visual coherence, A breaks its own segment colour code: the charts on slides 4, 5, 6 and 9 read A=blue, B=purple, C=orange, but the table on slide 3 assigns B=orange and C=purple, and the scoring table on slide 8 shifts again (Segment A row purple). B holds one encoding end to end — A=blue, B=orange, C=green on the slide 2 cards, the slide 4 table header, and the bars on slides 6 and 8 — with a consistent footer rule and NN/10 pagination. On communicative effectiveness B is also better structured: slide 2 states the call with the three headline numbers as cards, slide 3 makes the weighting explicit in a criterion/weight/what-it-measures table before any scoring, slide 8 shows the resulting scores, slide 9 numbers the recommendation, slide 10 is a dated 90-day path. A covers the same ground but spends three near-identical single-metric bar slides (4, 5, 6) with large empty plot areas on data already summarised in its slide 3 table, and its weight donut on slide 7 is a weaker read than B's weights table. B's flaw is that slide 5 puts CAGR % and capability-overlap % on one axis, which mixes units; A's flaw list is longer and lower in the rubric. On distinctiveness both are unremarkable: A's navy cover and purple accent are marginally more considered than B's default blue/orange/green, but that sits above the level where B has already won.

Neither deck has an integrity failure I can see — no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap on either. At level 2 both are readable, but A leans on very small type in more places: the source and footer lines on pages 4-6 and the caption under the weighted-score table on page 8 are near-illegible, and the three stacked criteria bars on page 7 (25% / 35% / 40%) squeeze body copy into thin strips, one of them reversed out on a dark fill. B's only comparable contrast risk is the white small-caps 'SEGMENT B' / 'SEGMENT C' labels on the orange and green cards on page 2. At level 3 both hold a consistent segment colour code (B: blue/orange/green; A: blue/purple/orange) through tables, cards and charts, and both repeat kicker, footer and page number. B breaks its own code once — the grouped bars on page 5 use blue for 'growth' and green for 'capability overlap', colours that mean Segment A and Segment C everywhere else — while A keeps colour meaning stable throughout. Both clear the integrity bar — nothing clipped, no placeholders, no overlaps in either deck — and both are legible, so the decision is made at levels 3–5. Integrity: neither shows overflow, placeholders or overlap; A's page 3 comparison table and B's page 3 table both render fully. Coherence: A repeats a consistent system — rule-under-heading, consistent left-aligned heading scale, a single table style with a light header rule — across all five pages; B mixes a black-filled table header on page 3 against otherwise hairline styling elsewhere, and its page-1 KPI stack (-4 pts / 38% / 61% run vertically with captions above and below) reads as three unrelated hand-placed blocks rather than a set. Communicative effectiveness: A wins clearly. A's page-1 KPI row is a true three-across comparison band with unit suffixes (4 pts, 38 %, 61 %) and captions in one register, immediately answering the brief's three headline numbers; A's headings state conclusions ('The problem is relevance, not price' appears in B too, but A carries this further with 'Recommendation', 'Risks to Manage', 'What Would Change This Recommendation'), and A's option table has explicit dimension rows (core lever, primary risk addressed, margin trajectory, time to results, reversibility) that make the trade-off decidable. B's table covers similar ground but with fewer decision-relevant rows and a heavier, less readable treatment. Both fully answer the 'what would change the recommendation' requirement. Craft/distinctiveness: A's title block (title + italic subtitle 'Defending relevance without gutting the P&L', then a metadata stack of Prepared for / Date / Status) reads as an authored consulting document; B's page 1 opens with a generic title and a bare 'Prepared for the Marketing Director — September 2026' line and then a wall of summary text before the KPIs, which is closer to a filled-in template. Both are generic-leaning — no brand colour, no chart, a single accent-free grey palette — but A's metadata block, KPI band and consistent section rules give it more intent. A is sendable; B would need the KPI band rebuilt and the page-3 table restyled first.

A fails at level 1 (integrity) in ways B does not. On A page 1 the 'Workstream / Delivered vs. Status target / What's blocking it' table has a collided header — 'Delivered vs.' and 'target' wrap into 'Status', and the IT row's blocker text 'Legacy-platform retirement decision not' is cut off at the cell/page boundary. The same header collision repeats at the top of A page 2, where an orphaned fragment 'taken' sits alone under an otherwise empty header row — a table split mid-cell across the page break. A page 3 opens with an orphan fragment 'different workstream' floating above the section heading. A's decision table on page 2 also shows a mangled owner cell ('Programme SponsorNext Steering (Transformation Committee SRO)') where two columns have run together. B shows no clipping, no orphaned fragments and no column collisions across its three pages; its tables (plan/delivered/% of plan on pages 1–2, the three-decision table on page 3) are dark-header banded tables that repeat identically and close with a 'Total recoverable this quarter 4.5' row.

Above integrity, B also wins on coherence and communicative effectiveness. B carries a running header ('Cost Programme Review — Month 14 Update') and a footer ('Confidential — prepared for the Transformation Office') on every page; A has neither, so its pages do not read as one document. B's headings state conclusions ('The programme is EUR 9m behind plan, and the shortfall sits in two workstreams', 'Three decisions this quarter recover half the shortfall', 'If nothing changes'), whereas A's are labels ('1. Where the shortfall sits', '2. The recovery: three decisions, this quarter'). B units its columns explicitly ('Plan to date (EURm)', 'Delivered (EURm)', 'Unlocks (EURm)') and gives each decision an owner and a due date; A's KPI strip is the better single element on either document (four large figures €46m/€19m/€28m/68% with labels), but B's two-stat treatment (46 EURm / 19 EURm / 68%) covers the same ground without A's table damage.

Both are generic in the same way — a Word-default serif-free report with a stat row and banded tables; neither has a distinctive visual idea, and B's 'EURm' set as a small superscript-ish unit beside 46 and 19 is awkward. B is simply the one that renders cleanly and could go to the transformation office unchanged.

A fails at the integrity/legibility level in ways B does not. On A page 1 the workstream table's columns collide: the header reads "Delivered vs.Status target" as one run-on string, and the body cells render "118%Ahead of plan", "41%Stalled", "33%Stalled" with no gutter between the percentage and the status column — two data columns visually fused. The last row of that table is also cut mid-sentence at the page break ("Legacy-platform retirement decision not"), and page 2 opens with the table header repeated over an almost-empty row containing the single orphan word "taken". The same collision recurs in A's decision table on page 2, where the Owner and Deadline cells overlap into "Programme SponsorNext Steering (Transformation Committee SRO)", making the owner and the deadline unreadable as separate facts — and this is the row that names the accountability fix, i.e. the most important cell in the document. A's page 2 also ends with a paragraph broken mid-clause ("exactly the same way, on a" / "different workstream."), which is a legitimate flow but lands awkwardly right under the table. B has no clipping, no overlap and no orphaned cells: its workstream table splits across pages 1–2 but repeats its header row cleanly, and both tables (Workstream/Plan/Delivered/% of plan, and Decision/Owner/Unlocks/Due) have dark header bands with clear column separation and a summed total row. B is also stronger above the integrity line: its page-1 heading states the conclusion ("The programme is EUR 9m behind plan, and the shortfall sits in two workstreams"), the three display figures 46 EURm / 19 EURm / 68% are labelled with units and captions, the page-2 heading states the recovery conclusion ("Three decisions this quarter recover half the shortfall"), and a consistent confidentiality footer repeats on all three pages. A's section titles are neutral labels ("1. Where the shortfall sits", "3. What happens if nothing changes") rather than conclusions, and it carries no footer. Both share the same weakness — a sparse page 3 with a large empty lower half — and both are only moderately distinctive: B is a competent house style with banded tables and a KPI strip, A is closer to an unstyled Word default with hairline tables. Neither is so specific to this brief that it couldn't be reskinned for another programme, but B is the only one of the two I would send unchanged.

Both clear level 1 and 2: no clipping, placeholders or overlaps in either, and body type is comfortably readable at letter size with an obvious single-column reading order. The separation starts at level 3 and widens above it. A is coherent but thin: its four-up KPI strip on page 1 (5.9% / 41% / 68% / $1.5M) has ragged caption depth — '+2.5 pts vs. 4 quarters ago' wraps to two lines while the others sit on one, so the baseline under the strip breaks — and pages 2 and 3 carry no running identifier at all, so the three sheets only cohere by typeface. B repeats a header ('Meridian Fitness Group · Churn Diagnosis') and a footer ('Confidential — prepared for the leadership team · September 2026') on all three pages, and reuses one table treatment (dark header band, footnote line beneath) for both the cohort table on page 2 and the revenue build on page 3, so repeated elements actually repeat. At level 4 B is clearly stronger: its title states the conclusion ('Why Churn Doubled — and the Two Fixes Already Proven to Work') where A's page-1 title only restates the metric ('Member Churn Diagnosis: From 3.4% to 5.9%'); B opens with a labelled Executive summary, and each table carries a source/derivation footnote ('*Derived from the reported four-point gap at sites that added a staffed onboarding session') and a takeaway line under the revenue table, while A's page-2 stat trio (2,250 / $124K / $1.5M) is explained only in the prose that follows and its cohort table has no note on where the retention figures come from. B's page-3 metric table also shows the arithmetic from 20,000 joins through to the $1.23M figure, which A asserts without a visible build. At level 5 B reads as a prepared deliverable (prepared-for line, confidential footer, numbered recommendations with a sequencing paragraph); A reads closer to a generic report template with the blanks filled — the KPI strip and lone table would look identical for any other diagnosis. B's cost is density: page 3 stacks a nine-row table, a two-item numbered list and a sequencing paragraph with little air, and page 1 is paragraph-heavy before the first stat. That is a level-5 refinement complaint, not a level-3 failure, so it does not offset B's advantages.

Both are clean, three-page Word documents with no clipping, overflow, or placeholder text, and both are legible at 11pt body with a running header/footer, so Levels 1–2 are a wash. The separation starts at Level 3 and 4. B (first image) uses a consistent device across all three pages: a dark-header table on p2 (cohort retention with a 'Gap vs. full-price' column) repeated as the dark-header metric table on p3 (revenue-at-stake build), plus a large-figure KPI pair on p1 (5.9% ▲ +2.5 pts / 41% ▼ -27 pts) and a single '4 pts ▼' stat on p2 — each with a caption line underneath giving basis and comparison. That repeated dark-header table plus caption-under-figure pattern is genuine cross-page rhythm. A (second image) front-loads all four KPIs on p1 (5.9%, 41%, 68%, $1.5M) and then never repeats the device again; p2's '2,250 / $124K / $1.5M' row is a second, differently-styled stat block, and p3 is pure prose with no visual element at all, so the document decays from designed page to plain memo. A's one table on p1 (12-month vs 12-month churn) also has an unstyled/light header, which does not match anything else in the file.

On communicative effectiveness B is also ahead: its p3 metric table shows the revenue arithmetic line by line (20,000 new members, 85% on promo, 7,480 expected to remain at full-price rate vs 4,510 at actual, 2,970 shortfall, €69 monthly dues, 6 months average tenure, €1.23M) so the $1.5M-class number is auditable, and it carries an explicit basis note under it. A asserts $1.5M and $124K/month and only explains the mechanics in paragraph form on p2, which is harder to check. B's recommendations on p3 are numbered with bolded lead-ins ('Make staffed onboarding standard at every site', 'Tie the promotional offer itself to onboarding completion') and close with a sequencing line; A's two recommendations are also bolded and numbered but the second one runs to the end of p3 as an undifferentiated block.

Against B: its p1 title is set over two lines with noticeably loose leading and the executive summary paragraph is a dense unbroken block; A's p1 title and lead are tidier and its p2 prose reads more fluently. And A's four-KPI opening row is a stronger single hero moment than B's two-KPI pair. But that is a Level-5 polish advantage that does not outrank B's better Level-3 consistency and Level-4 auditability.

Genericness: both are recognisably 'consulting memo with KPI row and a table' and neither would be mistaken for a bespoke identity — no chart, no colour beyond black/grey, no fitness-sector cue anywhere. B is marginally less generic because the dark-header tables and the caption-under-stat convention are at least a chosen, repeated system rather than defaults; A's p3, being wall-to-wall body text, is the most template-interchangeable page across both documents. Neither is something I would send unchanged with my name on it — both need a chart of the four-quarter churn trend and the cohort gap, which the brief practically demands and neither provides.

Integrity: A fails at level 1. Page 6 is a near-empty page carrying a single two-line orphan paragraph ('The recommendation is not to replace brokers with digital...') stranded at the top of an otherwise blank sheet — a widow that the author clearly did not intend as a page. Page 3 of A also has an integrity smell: the 'Period / Broker policies / Digital policies / Combined acquisition cost' table is immediately followed by a second header row ('Period / Gross saving vs today / Transition investment / Net effect') inside what reads as one continuous table block, so two different schemas are stacked with no separation — the reader cannot tell where one table ends. B has no clipped, empty or orphaned page: all four pages carry full content, each with a repeated 'Distribution Strategy Assessment' header and a 'Confidential — Internal distribution planning use only' footer.

Legibility: both are small-type walls, but B's body text is set marginally larger and its tables have visible header shading; A's page 4 investment table and page 3 tables are the smallest type in either document.

Visual coherence: B repeats a header/footer on every page, A has none — so A's pages 2-6 read as loose sheets. Both use the same oversized-numeral device (A: '78% / 57% / 9%' on page 1 and 'Year 3 / +EUR 9,000' on page 3; B: '78% / 9% / €96 / €41' on page 1 and 'Year 2' on page 3), but B's four-KPI row is more evenly weighted and its 'Year 2' callout on page 3 is a single clean statement, whereas A's page-3 callout splits into two large elements with two long captions underneath that fight each other.

Communicative effectiveness: both answer the payback-year question explicitly (A: Year 3, +EUR 9,000; B: Year 2), and both label units in EUR. B's page-2 'Recommended channel mix, year by year' table is the clearer artefact — one row per year with all three channels and policy counts in parentheses — versus A's page-3 mix table which repeats 13% 'other channels' four times without policy counts. B's page-2 investment table names the columns as spend/broker-equivalent/investment/net position, which is the actual payback arithmetic; A splits the same argument across two stacked half-tables on page 3.

Craft: neither is distinctive — both are single-column body-copy documents with one KPI row and a big-number callout. B wins on discipline (running header, footer, consistent table styling); A wins nothing that offsets the blank page 6.

Because A fails at level 1 (orphan page 6, ambiguous stacked table on page 3) and B does not, B is the document to send, by a clear margin. Neither is client-ready without edits — B's page 3 body text runs to a hard right edge with a long paragraph on adverse selection that should be broken up.

Genericness: both are highly generic. Strip the numbers from either and you have a stock consulting memo — a title page with three or four big statistics, a table or two, a bold pull-number, and a bulleted recommendation list. Nothing in the typography, no diagram of the broker-to-digital funnel, no chart of the three-year curve, no insurer-specific visual identity. B's running header and footer are the only elements that suggest a document series rather than a one-off template fill.

Integrity: neither clips, overflows or leaves placeholders. Both are legible — single-column body at a comfortable size, dark text on white, obvious reading order. The decision falls at level 3 and is close.

Visual coherence favours B. B carries a running header ("Distribution strategy assessment") and a footer ("Confidential — for distribution planning use only") on all four pages, so the repeated elements actually repeat. A shows no running header, footer or page number on any of its six pages, so each page floats free. B's worst break is the channel table on page 1 spilling one row ("Other channels / 13% / n/a") with a repeated header onto page 2 — routine and unobtrusive. A's worst is page 6: a single three-line closing paragraph ("The recommendation is not to replace brokers with digital…") stranded on an otherwise blank page, which a client sees instantly as a break that was never composed; A's page 2 also opens mid-numbered-list (items 3–4) and page 2 ends on the heading "The three-year channel mix" with its table pushed to page 3.

Communicative effectiveness slightly favours A: its per-year headings ("Year 1 — segment the book, not the panel", "Year 2 — make brokers users of the engine…") state conclusions, the payback table carries an explicit "Net effect" column, and it adds an assumptions section and next steps. But B answers the same brief compactly — the Year-by-year channel mix table, the investment-curve table with net position, the giant "Year 2" display with the caption tying it to the payback question, plus risks and a five-point recommendation summary — and its page 4 whitespace is a normal last-page tail rather than a stranded orphan. B's page 3 top paragraph is a dense full-measure wall of text, the one place where A's shorter blocks read better.

Since the coherence-level defect (A's orphan page and missing running furniture) outranks A's content edge, B is the one I would send, but only just.

Genericness: both read as the same "assessment memo" template — title, KPI band, headed sections, tables — and would look identical for a supply-chain or pricing brief with the numbers swapped. B has marginally more identity through the header/footer and the Year 2 display block; A's twin display stat ("Year 3 / +EUR 9,000") is its only distinctive gesture.

Both clear the integrity bar — no clipped text, no placeholders, nothing overlapping — but B has a real hierarchy defect that A does not: B's page 2 opens with three orphaned KPI figures (34/29/19 datapoints) stacked at the very top with no heading, no preceding lead-in, and no visible container, so the reader hits a naked number block before the section it belongs to; the same figures in A sit inside the executive summary on page 1 with captions ('Already collected for other purposes', 'Collectable within the year, with effort', 'Requires new measurement not yet in place'), which is where the audit committee expects the headline count. B also breaks its own type system: page 1's title 'CSRD Readiness Assessment' is centred with a centred subtitle and rule, while every subsequent page is left-aligned and numbered — a title page grafted onto a body that does not use it — and section 6 on page 4 runs onto page 5 with a bare orphan line ('should use estimates deliberately and label them as such') sitting above the section it continues. At level 4 A is materially stronger: the datapoint readiness table on page 3 is a full 12-row ESRS topic matrix with a Total row (82/34/29/19) that reconciles to the KPI band, and page 7 carries a real Milestone/Target timeline table plus an explicit 'Assumptions and Basis for This Assessment' block and a prepared-by/reviewed-by sign-off — exactly the artefacts an audit committee needs to challenge the work. B's equivalent table on page 3 covers only 7 topics and totals 34/29/19 without showing the 82, has no timeline, and no assumptions or sign-off block at all; its final page 6 ends on the decisions list with a large empty lower half. Where B is better is voice — it names Meridian Fabrication Group, FY2027, the 2028 filing cycle and specific Scope 3 categories (purchased goods, upstream transport, fuel-and-energy), so it reads written for one company; A is deliberately anonymised ('the Company') and its section headings ('What to build first — the next two quarters', 'What the first report will honestly not be able to say') are the more distinctive writing. Neither is distinctive at level 5 — both are single-column Word documents with one grey-header table and no chart — but A is the one I would send unchanged, on completeness of evidence and consistency of page furniture; B needs its KPI block re-anchored and its title page reconciled with the body first.

Both render cleanly at level 1–2: no clipped text, no placeholders, no overlap, and both use a legible serif/sans body at a sensible measure. The decision is made at levels 3–5.

Integrity: B is clean but page 6 ends after eight short numbered decisions with roughly two-thirds of the page empty, and page 5 leaves a large gap under the numbered list on 'What The First Report Will Honestly Not Be Able To Say'. A also has a soft page 6 (the 'What the first report will honestly not be able to say' section carries a stray orphaned 'for.' fragment at the top of the page, which is a real defect) but its pages are otherwise filled to a consistent depth. That fragment is A's one integrity blemish and it is small; B's white-space collapse is a rhythm problem rather than a break, so neither fails outright here.

Visual coherence: A is more consistent. It sets a repeated pattern — running heads, a metadata block on page 1 (Prepared for / Company profile / Reporting status / Date), a rule under each section head, tables with a shaded header row on pages 3 and 7 — and repeats it. B mixes a centred title page with left-aligned body pages, then puts three large stat numerals (34 / 29 / 19 datapoints) at the very top of page 2 with no framing, so they read as an orphaned fragment of a cover that spilled onto the next page. A places the same three figures deliberately as a three-up stat row inside the Executive Summary on page 1, labelled '34 of 82 / 29 of 82 / 19 of 82' with captions under each — the same data, composed rather than stranded.

Communicative effectiveness: A is clearly stronger. Its datapoint table on page 3 covers all ten ESRS topics with a Total row reconciling to 82/34/29/19, so the arithmetic in the brief is auditable on the page. B's table on page 3 lists only seven rows and totals 34/29/19 without the 82 column, so the reader cannot check the total against the headline. A also adds an 'Indicative Timeline to First Report' milestone table on page 7 and an 'Assumptions and Basis for This Assessment' block — exactly the material an audit committee needs to sign off, and directly responsive to 'what the first report will honestly not be able to say'. B has no timeline and no assumptions basis. A's headings are also more conclusion-bearing ('The Scope 3 Emissions Gap', 'What to build first — the next two quarters', 'What to estimate — and disclose as estimated'), while B's are numbered but generic ('3. Datapoint Readiness: Where The 82 Stand Today' is good; '5. What To Build First' is fine, but the set is less consistently a claim).

Craft: neither is distinctive — both are essentially a Word memo with one table. A edges ahead because the page-1 metadata block, the stat row and the signature block ('Prepared by: Sustainability & Finance Reporting Team / Reviewed by: Chief Financial Officer') on page 8 read as an intentional audit-committee document rather than a generic report shell. B's title-case headings ('What The First Report Will Honestly Not Be Able To Say') and unframed numerals feel more default.

Would I send either unchanged with my name on it? A, after removing the orphaned 'for.' at the top of page 6 — close to yes. B, no: I would first fix the stranded stat block on page 2 and fill or reflow pages 5–6.

Genericness: both are fairly generic — a serif-heading, single-column report that would look identical for a tax memo or an IT audit. A is marginally less so because its structure (metadata header, reconciling datapoint table, milestone table, assumptions basis, sign-off) is shaped by the specific brief; B's numbered-section skeleton would transplant to any topic with no visual change at all.

Both clear the integrity bar: nothing in either is clipped, empty or placeholder. A's only integrity-adjacent blemish is the hyphenated word-break in the page-2 pie title ("Incumbent concentra-tion leaves room to enter"), and the numbered condition list splitting so that item 3 lands alone at the top of page 4 above ~60% blank page; both are cosmetic, not broken content. Legibility is close — A's chart tick labels and the small italic chart notes on pages 2 and 3 are the smallest type in either document, while B's body copy is the more comfortable read at arm's length. Visual coherence is a wash: A repeats a consistent big-number KPI band (page 1: 340m / 61% / 0; page 2: EUR 2.1m / Month 26 / Month 34), consistent section rules and a repeated confidential footer; B repeats a running header and footer and a single dark-header table, and is tidier but flatter. The decision is made at level 4. A actually shows the payback the brief asked for: the page-3 cumulative cash-position line chart plots base and pessimistic cases against a zero line with the month-26/month-34 crossings visible, and it carries a stated basis ("Illustrative, based on EUR 2.1m invested over 18 months"); page 2 adds a market-size bar chart and an incumbent-share pie, each with a caption tying it to a takeaway, plus a scenario table with investment, period, break-even month and payback period. Its headings are conclusions ("Incumbent concentration leaves room to enter", "Conditions this recommendation depends on"). B answers the same brief with prose plus one four-column payback table and no visual at all — the payback is asserted, never shown — and its headings are category labels ("Market Opportunity", "Entry Plan & Economics", "Recommendation"). B's page-2 conditions are well written and bolded to their lead clause, which is its strongest passage, but the whole document reads as a two-page memo template with the blanks filled. A is the more distinctive artefact and the one that does the analytical work on the page; B is the more generic of the two.

Integrity: both render cleanly with no clipped or placeholder content, but A's page 4 is a near-empty page carrying only the tail of condition 3 and a short 'Recommended next steps' list, leaving ~55% of the page blank — a pagination blemish, not a break. B has no such orphan; its two pages are fully used. Neither has overlap or overflow, so both clear level 1, A with a minor demerit. Legibility: B's page 1 body sets long full-measure lines in a small serif-ish grey and its three KPI figures (EUR340m / 9% / 61%) sit as bare numerals with captions in very faint grey; A's same KPI band (EUR 340m / 61% / 0) uses heavier weight and darker captions and is easier to scan. Both are readable; A is more comfortable. Visual coherence: both are consistent internally; A adds a repeated red accent (rules, chart series, table header) that recurs on every page, and a consistent running footer 'Confidential — prepared for the Board of Directors'. B repeats a header/footer too but its page 2 table is the only styled object in the document, so the two pages don't feel like the same system. Communicative effectiveness is where the gap opens: the brief asks to show payback under both cases, and A actually shows it — page 3 carries a labelled cumulative cash-position chart with both series, axis units (EUR m, months since launch), a source/basis line ('Illustrative, based on EUR 2.1m invested over 18 months'), plus page 2's market-size bar chart and incumbent-concentration pie with a takeaway headline ('Nordic market size, growing ~9% a year'). B shows the payback only as a four-row table on page 2 and has no chart anywhere; its page 1 KPI trio is asserted with no visual. A's section headings also state conclusions ('Conditions this recommendation depends on', 'Payback: cumulative cash position by scenario'), and its KPI headline includes the '0 Finnish-language products offered by either incumbent' stat that is the actual wedge in the brief. B's headings are generic nouns ('Market Opportunity', 'Entry Plan & Economics'). Craft: A's chart on page 2 has a cramped pie title that wraps awkwardly ('concentra-tion' hyphenating mid-word) and the page-4 orphan is sloppy; B is tidier but blander. Because the decisive difference sits at level 4 and both are sound at 1–3, A wins clearly rather than decisively. Genericness: B reads as a template — a title, three big numbers, prose sections and one table would look identical for any market-entry brief. A is somewhat more brief-specific: the '0 Finnish-language products' KPI, the two-scenario payback curve and the named Stockholm-office conditions could not be swapped into another deck unchanged, though its overall grid is still conventional consulting-memo.

A fails at Level 1 in a way that outranks everything above it: page 7 is entirely blank — no header, no footer, no content — a trailing empty page that would go out to a steering committee as-is. A also splits the deferral table badly across pages 5–6: the 'Synergy captured' row ends page 5 and page 6 opens with the orphaned fragment 'captured, not a shift in timing.' above a repeated 'Area | Effect of a 12-month deferral' header, so the reader meets a dangling clause before any context. B has no empty page and no broken row; its weakest moment is page 5, where 'Recommendation' carries a single short paragraph over mostly white space — a thin tail, but a page that renders what the author meant.

On coherence B is also ahead: every B page carries the same running head ('Alderwood Facilities Group · Confidential') and footer ('Confidential — Prepared for the Steering Committee'), so repeated elements actually repeat. A has no header, footer, page number or confidentiality mark on any of its seven pages, and its page-1 KPI strip has four captions of wildly uneven depth (the 40% caption runs four lines against one line for 'customer overlap'), which makes the baseline under the strip ragged. B's tables use a consistent dark header band with white type on pages 2 and 4; A's use light grey shading on page 2 and page 4 but the page 5/6 deferral table has a different, unshaded treatment.

A is not without merit above the failure line: its page 2 synergy table adds a 'What unlocks it' column, its page 4 milestone table adds 'Definition of done', and the €3.3m callout on page 5 is the single most distinctive element in either document — it makes the deferral cost the visual climax, which is exactly the brief's hardest ask. B answers the same point with plain bullets on page 4. But that advantage sits at Levels 4–5 and cannot rescue a blank page and a broken table row at Level 1.

On genericness both are moderately templated — stacked headings, two shaded tables, a KPI strip — but B is more clearly made for this brief: it names Alderwood and Brackenfield throughout, ties the milestone table's third column to 'Synergy at run-rate' (+€1.5m, +€3.5m, €4.92m 60%, €8.2m 100%), and phrases page 4's title as a conclusion ('What a One-Year Deferral Costs'). A anonymises the parties to 'the Group' and 'the acquired business', which reads more like a fill-in-the-blank shell despite the stronger callout.

Integrity decides this. A ends with a completely blank page 7, and its deferral table splits a row across pages 5–6 so page 6 opens with the stranded fragment "captured, not a shift in timing." sitting under a repeated header with no label cell — a visible break in the artefact. B has no clipping, no empty page and no broken row; its weakest moment is page 5, where the two-sentence "Recommendation" sits alone on an otherwise empty page, which is under-filled but not a failure. At legibility both hold, though A's body copy on pages 2–3 and its hairline tables run noticeably smaller and tighter than B's. Visual coherence again favours B: a running header ("Alderwood Facilities Group · Confidential") and footer on every page, one navy accent used consistently for section headings and for the dark table header bands on the synergy tranche table (p2) and the milestones table (p4), and a rule-anchored stat block on p1. A carries no page furniture at all — no footer, no pagination — and its headings sit at near-identical weight, so "Phase 1 — Stabilise, decide and harvest" (p3) and "Overlap and synergy profile" (p2) read at the same level despite being different ranks. A wins clearly at level 4 and only there: its milestones table (p4) adds a "Definition of done" column, its deferral table (p5–6) breaks the loss into dual-running cost, depot rationalisation, customer risk, people risk and time value of money rather than B's bullet list on p4, the €3.3m ▼ callout on p5 answers the deferral question in one figure, and the six numbered "Recommendations to the steering committee" on p6 are far more actionable than B's single closing paragraph. A also lands the only genuinely assertive title in either document, "The dispatch migration is the constraint" (p5); B's headings ("The Synergy Case and Its Dependency") are closer to labels.
